tier_reason: The author's bench.md alone is only tier C: its results are graphs, the code snippet is partial and the flags are not stated. Two independent third-party suites include spp::sparse_hash_map and show it beating libstdc++ std::unordered_map: Ankerl 2022 (martinus/map_benchmark; clang++ 13 -O3 -march=native; i7-8700) and Tessil's 2017 shootout. That keeps it at B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Ankerl 2022, an independent suite with normalized runtimes and the same hash for both maps (the verifier computed the ratios std::unordered_map / spp from the page's table data): geometric mean over all tests 1.98x (mumx) and 2.03x (robin_hood::hash); number find 2.35-2.51x; string find 1.52-1.82x; random insert & erase 1.18-1.31x. With identity std::hash, spp times out in the random insert & erase and number-find tests. Tessil 2017 shootout raw CSV (Clang 5.0 with libstdc++, 200K-3M entries, ratios computed by the verifier): successful lookups 1.11-3.31x faster; misses 1.15-5.60x faster; inserts 0.61-1.47x (slower on string keys). The author's bench.md (graphs only) says insert is 'as fast as the two std::unordered_map implementations', lookup is 'faster than all other alternatives, except for dense_hash_map', and delete is 'outperformed only by dense_hash_map'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ankerl 2022: clang++ 13, -O3 -march=native. (Author's bench.md: g++ 4.8.4 and Boost 1.55, flags not stated.)
corrections.hardware: Ankerl 2022: Intel i7-8700 locked at 3200 MHz, Manjaro Linux. (Author's bench.md: VirtualBox VM with 5.8GB RAM, Ubuntu written as '14.02'.)
corrections.caveats: In Ankerl 2022, spp times out with identity std::hash on integer-key insert/erase and find tests, so it is sensitive to hash quality. Its copy is slow, and its memory use is about 3x lower than std::unordered_map. The author's bench.md is a graph-only write-up from about 2016 on a VM. The README now recommends greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap instead of sparsepp.
